name: Pallavaneswarar Temple, Poompuhar
deity: Shiva as Pallavaneswarar, with the goddess Soundaryanayaki
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Chola port of Kaveripoompattinam, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with later additions
dynasty: Chola country; later Tamil patrons (builders not firmly sourced)
summary: Pallavaneswarar is the Shiva temple of old Kaveripoompattinam, the Tiruppallavaneecharam of the Tevaram, standing near the Kaveri's mouth and remembered as the birthplace of the saint-poet Pattinathar.

sections.history: Poompuhar, at the mouth of the Kaveri on the Bay of Bengal, was the great port of the early Cholas, known in the old literature as Kaveripoompattinam or Puhar. In the Tevaram hymns its Shiva temple is called Tiruppallavaneecharam, and the child-saint Sambandar sang its praise, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, counted as the tenth such shrine on the northern bank of the Kaveri. Tradition says a Pallava king worshipped here and found liberation, and from him the Lord took the name Pallavaneswarar. The temple is held to stand on the birthplace of the merchant-saint Pattinathar, so that the shrine has long been remembered as much for his renunciation as for the port that rose and fell around it.
sections.architecture: This is a modest, intimate temple facing east beneath a five-tiered rajagopuram, with a single enclosing prakaram and two corridors, and, unusually, no flagstaff. The linga in the sanctum is revered as self-manifested, and the goddess Soundaryanayaki, the beautiful one, has her own shrine. In the prakaram, Murugan stands with his consorts Valli and Deivanai, and the peacock that normally accompanies him is absent. The niches of the sanctum wall hold two forms of Durga, and Ganesha and Chandikeswara are also honoured. A separate shrine to Pattinathar faces north. The sea, which once lapped the old port at the temple's feet, now lies a few kilometres to the east.
sections.legends: Several traditions gather here. One tells that Kubera, lord of wealth, and the sage Kalava worshipped Shiva in this place, and that a Pallava king also prayed here and attained liberation. The best loved story is that of Pattinathar. Born in the port to a Shaiva couple, Sivanesar and Gnanakamalambikai, and named Tiruvenkadar, he grew into a wealthy sea-trader. When a chest he took to hold great treasure was opened, it contained only a cake of dung and husk, with a message that not even a broken needle follows one beyond death. Tiruvenkadar understood, gave up his wealth, and walked the roads of the Tamil country as the renunciant Pattinathar, finally attaining liberation at Tiruvottriyur.
sections.festivals: The temple's great festival honours the devotee rather than the deity: the twelve-day Pattinathar festival in the month of Aadi, in July or August, is the temple's principal celebration, and no separate Brahmotsavam is held for Shiva himself. Vaikasi Visakam in May or June is observed for Murugan. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are kept as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Poompuhar rewards a slow visit. Come first to the sanctum of Pallavaneswarar and then to the shrine of Soundaryanayaki, and take time in the prakaram to find the peacock-less Murugan and the two Durgas. Many devotees pause at the north-facing shrine of Pattinathar, whose verses on the brevity of worldly wealth seem well placed in this once-wealthy harbour town. Afterward, walk toward the coast where the Kaveri meets the sea, and imagine the ships that once crowded these quays. The temple itself is small and quiet, and rarely crowded outside festival days.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to around midday and again from late afternoon until about half past seven in the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Poompuhar lies on the Coromandel coast, about 20 km from Sirkazhi and 24 km from Mayiladuthurai, which has the nearest main railway station. Regular buses connect Poompuhar with both towns, and the temple is in the town itself. The nearest airport listed is Tiruchirappalli, so most visitors travel on by road.
